HONGKONG'S VOICE
It is now over seven weeks since there took place in Sharnen incidents which, so far as the Chinese involved were concerned, can only be described as an open act of warfare. Since then, a movement has been directed from Canton which has brought entirely to an and the trade of British arms with South China and affected adversely the Chinese but as the weeks have passed and there still remains a deadlock apparently even as regards the constitution of the Commission which is to enquire into this and other matters, the query has grown more insistent "what is the British Government going to do about it?"

Take, for instance, the case of European importing and exporting firms in Hongkong. In the volume of business done in the ordinary course with the Chinese there is proof of the desire on the part of China for the materials that British firms supply. Through the machinations of an alien Power the Chinese are prevented from exercising a free choice, and so long as the Canton Government remains under the influence of Bolshevist agitators it is doubtful if any trade at all in the generally accepted sense of the word will be possible. Meanwhile, with the gravity of the situation as regards financial obligations increasing with every week that the present state of affairs is allowed to continue, the merchant has cause to wonder if there is not something wrong with an organisation which does not permit of Hongkong making direct representations to the Home Government on matters concerning South China, unless they occur within the territory within its jurisdiction. It is this lack of coordination which has been responsible to a considerable extent for the delay which may mean financial ruin for firms even of considerable standing.
Shameen being under the Foreign Office, the Consul General there has to conduct all negotiations through the Ambassador in Peking, he in turn has to negotiate with a Government which is supposed to have recognised a southern Government

In any event, representations it wishes to make officially, must go through the Colonial Office which has no power but may, if it chooses, pass such on to the Foreign Office. Thus it comes about that when Hongkong desires to represent its views to the Home Government direct on happenings at Shameen and Canton which directly concerns it, for Canton is South China so far as business is concerned and trade with Canton is almost entirely directed from Hongkong, a public meeting has to be called and cablegrams despatched on the initiative of the conveners.

It would perhaps be too much to expect the Home Government to establish what might become an awkward precedent in placing a Crown Colony under the administration of the Foreign Office, but Hongkong's opinion must in the future be more clearly voiced in councils of deliberation at Home on affairs concerning it. Such a vital matter may well be one to commend to the consideration of our new Governor, the Hon. Mr. C. Clementi.
A BEGINNING.

Straws are said to show which way the wind is blowing. The first of what we may call a series of settlements in the north, may be taken to show that a beginning is being made in a return to reason. After three weeks' negotiations an agreement has been reached which provides, for resumption of work at the Japanese Cotton Mills. Nine companies, owning forty factories and employing 50,000 hands, are concerned. Three weeks may seen a considerable length of time in which to settle a presumably simple matter—the antagonism having been on one side only. The agreement puts the Japanese owners in a very creditable light. It must, at the outset, cause the indifferent and the ignorant to think that capitalists are not so bad as Bolsheviks and a certain type of Socialist would have us believe. The owners of the mill where rioting took place have offered the wounded and relatives of those killed $10,000. We trust this offer will not be taken as a sign of weakness. It seems easy to convince the unlettered, untutored, and unthinking mass of labour in China that its ends can easily be attained by a "little" strike, and possibly a "little" bloodshed. If such is the case it should be quickly contradicted. Think of Chinese capitalists acting similarly! The further clauses of the agreement suggest that there is not one of them that could not have been obtained by peaceful, if persistent representations. The Labour movement in China is likely to approximate to that which exists elsewhere: numbers of guilds or unions, controlled by paid officers, who, in order to "earn their salt" are likely to exert undue influence and willfully foment unnecessary trouble. Peaceful representations would, in time, have gained such things as increase in wages where such was found to be necessary; the recognition of organised Labour Unions; and the other things included in the agreement. The vexed question of strike pay enters into the matter and here there seems a diplomatic victory for both sides. No strike pay is to be given, but as the reluctant strikers suffered through the loss of wages during the long strike, the millowners will compassionately extend reasonable help to the workers. Hongkong should be particularly interested in this part of the agreement; for it establishes a precedent from which it will be difficult to get away, if, and we do not suggest it, it is desired to do so. For Hongkong cannot ignore the fact that many of its strikers have been reluctant, although it can be argued, and probably proved, that they suffered no particularly big loss, seeing that many of them have been shepherded in Canton and enjoyed notoriety so much enamoured of certain types of Chinese minds. The money question is likely to play a great part in any effort at settlement which may come from the other side and those called upon to negotiate should know what they are likely to think about before entering any meeting room. lions or lions of Judah has brought forth a flood of learned comment and research into a subject seemingly devoid of great historical interest. However, an eminent authority now comes into the field with the assertion that the English lion is not English at all, but French. It is held to have come from Aquitaine, that land beloved by James Branch Cabell, where the kings of England once held large properties as dukes of Aquitaine. It is further held by heraldic experts that there is no definitely English beast for heraldic purposes. There was the great Dragon of King Arthur, but his slaying by St. George has rather ruined him for public purposes. If the English lion is really French, there is rather a touch of humour in the fact that Landseer's polite-looking lion was erected at the base of the column dedicated to the memory of Nelson, the "scourge of the French."

When the late Lord Northcliffe, then Alfred Harneworth, started Answers, his colleagues in the enterprise were Edward Markwick and Captain Benmont, both then resident, as Harmsworth was, in small villas at South Norwood. It was believed the arrangement between the three was that Captain Benmont supplied the capital, Markwick the technical knowledge, and Harmsworth the ideas. However, in the end, Harmsworth got rid of his two colleagues, both of whom strongly resented the process. Much to Harmsworth's credit, when his income began to run into great figures he amply compensated Markwick for his services. Whether Benmont participated is not known, but it would not be surprising if he did.
When Northcliffe was in Hongkong a then member of the staff of one of the papers tried to get him to visit his particular paper's office. He thought the office so unique, that Northcliffe would be impressed with it—in a certain direction let it be added. But here was nothing doing. Northcliffe, spent part of an evening with the present M.O.H., Dr. Pearse at the Hongkong Club—doubtless a very interesting time. There is growing rapidly at Ann Arbor a remarkable collection of manuscripts of the Middle Ages and of popyri of the more ancient world. To these will be added results of the recent excavations in many places. One of these is the site of the ancient Karniis in Egypt. Prof. F. W. Kelsey, director of the university's excavations, has just returned to the United States. He reports that since December 1924, there have been found at Karniis more than 2,000 objects disclosing the life and culture of the city that flourished in the centuries just preceding and following the birth of Christ. The site of the city is no dry that the preservation of perishable substances has been perfect.
Since last December, more than 300 houses have been uncovered and more than 1,000 rooms have been cleared of debris and sand. Here are some of the articles found: 450 Greek popyri, a small library dating from the second to the fifth centuries in large collection of glass vessels, fifty examples of basketry, textiles showing ancient fabrics from the line to course weaves like turban, 100 examples of wooden tools, large numbers of terra cotta objects, 200 lamps, great numbers of coins, farming implements, perilous prevailed sets of harnesses for donkey and swans, a big bakery with pales of coarse flat loaves of bread and a large roll for grinding.
